species.name: Smooth-coated otter
species.habitat: Mangroves, reservoirs, ponds and urban canals
species.fact: Social family groups use both natural and highly urban waterways.
species.rarity: Regular at some waterways; nationally threatened
species.summary: A social water-loving mammal that has returned to Singapore’s waterways. Family groups can live close to people, but they still need space to feed, rest and raise pups.
species.identification: A long brown body, short smooth fur and a paler throat and underside. It is larger than the Asian small-clawed otter; do not identify the species from size alone.
species.diet: Mainly fish, with other aquatic prey.
species.activity: Active on land and in water; sightings vary with the group and site.
species.behaviour: Travels and feeds in family groups. Groups use scent and calls and may compete with other families over territory.
species.reproduction: Pups are raised in sheltered dens, with adults attending them. Keep away from resting and den areas even if no adult is visible.
species.singapore: Uses mangroves, reservoirs, ponds and urban canals. Frequent sightings at one waterway do not change its national Endangered status.
species.ecologicalRole: An aquatic predator connecting waterways and adjacent land habitats.
species.pressures: Road crossings, disturbance and unsafe encounters can affect urban families. Connected, usable waterways remain important.
species.watch: Keep your distance and do not block the route between the group and water. Keep dogs leashed and never feed otters.

after.name: Asian koel
after.habitat: Fruiting trees in parks and woodland
after.rarity: Common; often heard rather than seen
after.fact: A koel chick can be raised by a crow after its egg was laid in the crow’s nest.
after.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2016
after.summary: The loud morning caller many Singapore residents know by sound. It is a cuckoo whose chicks are raised in another bird’s nest.
after.identification: Males are glossy black with a pale bill and red eyes. Females are brown with pale spots and bars, so the two sexes look quite different.
after.diet: Mainly fruit, with other food taken opportunistically.
after.activity: Diurnal; calling can begin early in the morning.
after.behaviour: Often stays in foliage around fruiting trees. Its repeated call is more conspicuous than the bird itself.
after.reproduction: Lays eggs in other birds’ nests, including crows’ nests. The host adults provide the chick’s care: this is called brood parasitism.
after.singapore: Common in secondary woodland, gardens, parks and other urban greenery. It is a native resident, not an introduced noise-making species.
after.ecologicalRole: A fruit consumer and brood parasite in the local bird community.
after.pressures: Loss of fruiting trees removes food. Managing noise complaints should not involve disturbing wildlife nests.
after.watch: Listen from a distance and avoid playback. Do not search for or interfere with a host nest.

after.name: Asian leaf turtle
after.habitat: Forest streams
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.fact: The hatchling has a flattened shell densely patterned with dark spots; adults have a dark-brown shell.
after.summary: A secretive stream-associated turtle, listed as Critically Endangered in Singapore. Its subdued colours fit the shaded forest setting.
after.identification: An oval, dark-brown shell with a toothed rear edge; orange lines mark the dark head and neck. Hatchlings are flatter and more densely spotted than adults.
after.diet: An omnivore that eats both plant and animal material.
after.activity: NParks describes apparent nocturnal activity; detailed Singapore activity patterns remain poorly documented.
after.behaviour: Associated with forest streams and their banks. Limited sightings make this an animal to learn about without seeking out sensitive sites.
after.reproduction: Lays eggs; local nesting timing and clutch sizes have not been verified.
after.singapore: NParks documents catchment-forest records from 2006 and 2007. These are historical observations, while RDB3 (2024) retains the species as nationally Critically Endangered; neither is a current population census.
after.ecologicalRole: Its mixed diet connects plant material and animal prey within the forest-stream food web.
after.pressures: Habitat degradation and collection for food or trade are identified threats. Forest streams and surrounding cover need protection.
after.watch: Stay out of streams and leave turtles, eggs and cover undisturbed. Do not collect or release pet turtles into natural habitats.

after.name: Banded bullfrog
after.habitat: Gardens, built areas and temporary pools
after.fact: A threatened bullfrog can inflate its body to appear larger.
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.summary: A round-bodied frog often heard after rain in Singapore. It adapts well to gardens and built areas but is recorded by NParks as introduced here.
after.identification: A small head, rounded body and two broad pale bands against a darker back. It can inflate its body when threatened.
after.diet: Ants, termites and other small invertebrates.
after.activity: Mostly nocturnal; calling often follows rain.
after.behaviour: Shelters in covered places and can climb as well as move on the ground. Its low call may carry farther than expected from its size.
after.reproduction: Gathers near temporary pools or other still water to breed. Eggs develop into aquatic tadpoles before metamorphosis into frogs.
after.singapore: Common in gardens, parks and other built environments. Being well established is different from being native.
after.ecologicalRole: Consumes small invertebrates and is itself prey for other animals.
after.pressures: Traffic and loss of usable breeding water affect encounters locally. Do not introduce frogs or tadpoles to new sites.
after.watch: Listen after rain from a safe path. Leave adults, eggs and tadpoles in place.

after.name: Black-eyed litter frog
after.habitat: Forest floor and streams
after.rarity: Elusive; common within some forest habitat
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.fact: Researchers identify its rapid, rattling call even when the frog itself stays hidden.
after.summary: A small leaf-litter frog with conspicuous dark eyes and a surprisingly distinctive voice. Being common within a forest patch does not mean it is widespread across Singapore.
after.identification: Large head and black eyes, relatively short slender limbs, and grey or brown skin marked with irregular dark patches. The pale underside has dark speckling.
after.diet: Insectivorous, feeding on small animal prey in its forest-floor habitat.
after.activity: Mainly nocturnal.
after.behaviour: Lives among fallen leaves. Its rapid rattling call can be easier to notice than its camouflaged body.
after.reproduction: Has an aquatic tadpole stage. NParks describes the larvae as large and almost black; no verified Singapore clutch-size or fixed breeding-season estimate is supplied here.
after.singapore: Associated with the Central Nature Reserves and forest stream habitats. NParks surveys found it frequently in suitable forest, while RDB3 assesses it as nationally Near Threatened.
after.ecologicalRole: An insect predator within the forest-floor food web, with aquatic larvae linking the life cycle to water.
after.pressures: Maintaining connected, moist forest and its water habitats is important for this habitat-associated frog; local frequency should not be confused with habitat security.
after.watch: Observe without moving logs or leaves. Keep out of streams, avoid playback and flash, and leave amphibians and tadpoles untouched.

after.behaviour: Forages in trees and may join other birds at fruiting plants. Look high in the foliage and listen as well as watch.

after.ecologicalRole: Consumes fruit and insects in the canopy food web.
after.pressures: Retention of mature trees and food plants supports nesting and foraging.
after.watch: Watch feeding birds from the path. Avoid pointing out or approaching active nests.

after.name: Blue-eared kingfisher
after.habitat: Shaded forest streams and mangroves
after.rarity: Uncommon resident of wooded water margins
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.fact: Its nest is reached through a tunnel it digs into a stream bank.
after.summary: A small resident kingfisher of shaded waterways. Its strong blue-and-rust colours can disappear surprisingly well against dark water and forest cover.
after.identification: Around 16 cm long, with deep cobalt-blue upperparts and rich rusty underparts. Adult males have dark bills; females can show red on the lower bill or more extensively. It is smaller and darker blue than the Common Kingfisher.
after.diet: Small fish and aquatic invertebrates caught around sheltered water.
after.activity: Look for daytime perch-and-dive hunting beside shaded water; a full local daily activity pattern is not quantified here.
after.behaviour: May bob its head and flick its tail while watching from a perch. After a dive, it can beat captured prey against a branch before swallowing.
after.reproduction: Excavates a nesting tunnel in a forest-stream bank. This guide omits exact nest positions and does not extrapolate overseas clutch sizes or breeding months to Singapore.
after.singapore: Bird Society of Singapore lists it as an uncommon resident that favours dense woodland and mangroves. NParks has also documented use of the Eco-Link@BKE wildlife bridge; the bridge is not a public viewing site.
after.ecologicalRole: A small predator linking stream invertebrates and fish to the surrounding wooded food web.
after.pressures: Maintaining shaded waterways and undisturbed banks follows from its documented feeding and nesting needs. This is a habitat-based conservation recommendation, not a quantified local decline claim.
after.watch: Remain on public paths and give bank vegetation space. Do not clear branches for photographs, bait the bird, play calls or approach a burrow entrance.

after.name: Buffy fish owl
after.habitat: Forested waterways and mangroves
after.rarity: Uncommon resident; often hidden by day
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.fact: The pointed tufts on its head are feather ornaments, not exposed ears.
after.summary: A large owl adapted to hunting beside water. Singapore has a resident population, but daytime resting and night activity can make individual birds difficult to notice.
after.identification: Look for yellow eyes, outward-pointing feather tufts and warm brown plumage with dark streaks. The tufts are not its actual ears. Bird Society of Singapore gives an adult length of about 46–47 cm.
after.diet: Fish, crabs and frogs, with other small prey such as rats taken around banks.
after.activity: Mostly nocturnal; rests among tree foliage during the day.
after.behaviour: Often watches water from a low branch before swooping for prey. Its unfeathered lower legs and gripping feet suit this fishing lifestyle.
after.reproduction: A documented Singapore nesting observation found a chick in a bird's-nest fern in 2016. Such records establish local breeding, but do not provide a complete island-wide breeding calendar.
after.singapore: Associated with wooded streams, reservoirs and mangroves. NParks records it in the Central Catchment and Pulau Ubin; these are broad occurrence areas, not nest directions or guaranteed sightings.
after.ecologicalRole: Its diet links aquatic prey and land animals to a nocturnal predator in the same wetland food web.
after.pressures: NParks identifies illegal trapping as a threat. Keeping suitable trees and quiet water margins is a habitat-based conservation priority, not a measured population trend.
after.watch: Watch from open paths using binoculars. Avoid flash, prolonged torchlight, playback or crowding a resting bird. Never approach a nest or publish its precise position.

after.name: Changeable hawk-eagle
after.habitat: Forest, woodland and wooded edges
after.rarity: Resident; may be seen or heard near woodland
after.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2020
after.fact: Pale and dark hawk-eagles can belong to the same species; these colour forms are called morphs.
after.globalAssessmentNote: Published assessment: 2020, cited by The Peregrine Fund. The exact assessment date was not recovered; this is a dated reference, not a claim of the latest assessment.
after.summary: A resident forest raptor whose plumage can look dramatically different between individuals. It can be conspicuous above woodland while still depending on places to hunt and nest.
after.identification: Adults occur in pale and dark colour forms. Pale adults have streaked light underparts; dark adults are largely dark brown. Pale juveniles can show much cleaner white underparts. Its length is about 61–75 cm, so colour alone is insufficient for identification.
after.diet: Birds, small mammals and reptiles such as snakes and lizards; it may occasionally scavenge.
after.activity: Diurnal; hunts, perches and soars during the day.
after.behaviour: Often hunts by waiting quietly on a concealed perch, then making a short attack when prey comes within reach. It may also soar above wooded areas.
after.reproduction: Both partners construct a stick nest in a tall tree, lining it with greenery. Species accounts describe a single egg and prolonged care; breeding dates differ across its range and are not a Singapore schedule.
after.singapore: NParks records it in forest reserves and Pulau Ubin and highlights it in woodland birdwatching at Kranji Marshes. Bird Society lists it as a common resident; frequency of observation does not remove its national Vulnerable status.
after.ecologicalRole: A predator of several animal groups that links different parts of the woodland food web.
after.pressures: The Peregrine Fund identifies habitat loss, fragmentation and persecution across the species' range. These are range-wide pressures, not a measured Singapore population trend.
after.watch: Scan the canopy from public trails. Never bait a raptor or approach an occupied nest. Keep the bird's flight path clear and watch through binoculars.

after.name: Clouded monitor
after.habitat: Forest and wooded parks
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.fact: Nostril position helps tell the two common monitors apart: the clouded monitor's nostril sits farther back from the snout tip.
after.summary: A native monitor that is as comfortable climbing trees as exploring the forest floor. It generally favours land habitats more than the familiar water monitor.
after.identification: Brown with yellow spotting. Compared with a Malayan water monitor, the head is shorter, the tail more rounded and the nostril sits farther back, about midway between the eye and snout tip. Use several features together.
after.diet: Searches through leaf litter for worms and other invertebrates.
after.activity: Diurnal: active during daylight, as documented in local forest surveys.
after.behaviour: Forages on the ground and climbs trees. Its ability to use both levels is a useful reminder to look above ground as well as along paths.
after.reproduction: Lays eggs. Local nesting dates, clutch size and incubation periods are not asserted from unrelated captive accounts.
after.singapore: NParks describes it as relatively common in suitable habitats, including forest and wooded gardens. This does not mean it is equally frequent in every neighbourhood.
after.ecologicalRole: A predator of small ground-dwelling animals within the leaf-litter food web.
after.pressures: Retaining forest cover, leaf litter and climbing trees helps preserve its habitat. Its local Least Concern label does not remove the need for respectful encounters.
after.watch: Watch from a distance and allow it to pass. Never feed, corner or handle a monitor, and keep pets under control.

after.summary: A familiar kingfisher that is not limited to fishing. It watches from a perch and can hunt small land animals well away from water.

after.pressures: Loss of vegetation, perches and nesting cover reduces useful habitat.
after.watch: Use binoculars from a fixed point. Let the bird resume hunting rather than following it between perches.

after.name: Dugong
after.habitat: Coastal seas, estuaries and seagrass beds
after.rarity: Rarely seen in Singapore waters; no population estimate implied
after.summary: A marine mammal that grazes on seagrass. Singapore records link this quiet swimmer to shallow coastal waters and river mouths.
after.identification: A bulky grey-brown body, blunt bristled muzzle, paired front flippers and a fluked tail. It has no dorsal fin.
after.diet: Mainly seagrass, gathered from underwater meadows.
after.activity: Feeding and resting alternate; the local NParks account describes night feeding and daytime rest in deeper water.
after.behaviour: May travel alone, with another dugong or in small groups. It surfaces to breathe and remains fully aquatic.
after.reproduction: A female normally produces one calf after a pregnancy lasting about thirteen to fourteen months. She nurses the calf. These general life-history notes do not establish a Singapore breeding season.
after.singapore: NParks records it mainly from the north-eastern Johor Straits. Records also include Changi, Pulau Ubin, Pulau Tekong and Labrador. A recorded location does not guarantee a sighting.
after.ecologicalRole: Seagrass feeding connects coastal vegetation with the marine food web.
after.pressures: Boat propellers, fishing-net entanglement, water pollution and loss of seagrass feeding grounds threaten dugongs.
after.watch: Observe from shore where possible. Never chase, feed or approach an animal with a boat. Report a stranded animal to NParks or ACRES and follow their instructions.

after.habitat: Forest understorey
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.fact: The decisive 2008 rediscovery photographs showed the throat and chest markings needed to identify the species.
after.summary: A small hoofed forest browser with a rounded body and very slender legs. Its rediscovery on Pulau Ubin shows why an animal missing from casual sightings is not necessarily gone.
after.identification: Reddish-brown fur, pale underparts and contrasting throat markings. More robust than the lesser mousedeer; useful photographs show the neck and chest, not just apparent size. It has no antlers.
after.diet: Fallen fruit, tender leaves and other low-growing plant material.
after.activity: Mostly nocturnal; usually feeds quietly on the forest floor.
after.behaviour: Typically encountered alone while browsing or resting under cover. A published Singapore survey also recorded more than one animal together, so solitary does not mean never seen with another.
after.reproduction: Usually produces one well-developed young. Regional accounts describe a pregnancy of roughly five months; this is not a prediction of Singapore birth dates. Juveniles were documented during the Ubin rediscovery study.
after.singapore: Confirmed on Pulau Ubin in 2008 after a long gap in verified records. NParks still includes the species in its 2025 Ubin conservation work. Its limited Singapore distribution does not mean every suitable mainland forest contains it.
after.ecologicalRole: A forest-floor plant consumer and part of the food web linking vegetation to predators.
after.pressures: Habitat disturbance and fragmentation can affect its restricted local habitat. Hunting is a pressure across its wider range. Protecting forest cover and limiting disturbance support its persistence.
after.watch: Keep to permitted paths, observe quietly and never feed or pursue it. Leave dense undergrowth undisturbed and do not share exact resting locations.

after.name: Horsfield’s flying squirrel
after.habitat: Forest canopy
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.fact: Its gliding membrane stretches between all four limbs; the long tail is flattened rather than round and bushy.
after.summary: A nocturnal squirrel that glides between trees on a membrane joining its limbs. Its quiet life above the ground makes it much less conspicuous than the daytime squirrels in parks.
after.identification: Dark brown upperparts, a paler orange-buff or whitish underside and rusty edges to the gliding membrane. A rounded head, large eyes and long, flattened, feather-like tail complete its outline.
after.diet: Mainly fruit, with insects also listed in the NParks species account.
after.activity: Active at night; rests in a tree cavity by day.
after.behaviour: Climbs using sharp claws and spreads its membrane to glide. It depends on trees for feeding, shelter and travel. Detailed social behaviour remains poorly studied.
after.reproduction: Gives birth to live young, but the reviewed species account does not establish its mating system, breeding season or litter size. Values from larger flying squirrels are not substituted.
after.singapore: Recorded in Singapore's central forest reserves and in a wooded nature park outside them. Local records require careful identification; difficulty seeing a nocturnal animal is not a population estimate.
after.ecologicalRole: A canopy fruit consumer that also eats small invertebrates. Its precise contribution to seed dispersal in Singapore has not been quantified in the reviewed sources.
after.pressures: Loss of forest and suitable cavity-bearing trees removes shelter and foraging areas. Maintaining connected wooded habitat is important for a species that travels between trees.
after.watch: Observe from permitted routes and avoid flash, sustained spotlighting or disturbance of tree holes. Never lure an animal with food or enter closed areas to seek it.

after.habitat: Forest edges, mangroves and parks
after.fact: Its tail can rival the combined length of its head and body.
after.globalStatus: Endangered · 2025
after.summary: Singapore’s familiar forest-edge monkey is a social, adaptable native primate. Food left accessible by people can draw groups into close contact with visitors and homes.
after.identification: Brown-grey coat, relatively pale underside and a tail that can be as long as the head and body together. It differs from the dark, pale-banded langur.
after.diet: Fruit and other plant food, plus insects and other small animals.
after.activity: Mainly diurnal.
after.behaviour: Lives in groups organised around related females. It forages both in trees and on the ground and uses calls, expressions and grooming socially.
after.reproduction: Usually gives birth to one infant. Mothers carry and nurse young, which remain within the social group as they grow.
after.singapore: Commonly encountered in and around forest reserves and some parkland. Feeding changes natural foraging behaviour and increases conflict.
after.ecologicalRole: An omnivore and fruit consumer in forest food webs.
after.pressures: Food-conditioned behaviour, unsafe interactions and habitat fragmentation can create local problems, even for a nationally Least Concern species.
after.watch: Keep food out of sight, secure bags and give the group space. Do not stare, feed, tease or try to touch a monkey.

after.behaviour: Often solitary. Hunts mainly on the ground but is an able climber. A single photograph may not be enough to rule out a domestic cat.

after.habitat: Mature forest streams
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.fact: Its angular outline and brown colouring help a motionless frog disappear among fallen leaves.
after.summary: A leaf-shaped ambush hunter from Singapore's mature forests. Its camouflage is so effective that a call may reveal a frog that the eye has missed.
after.identification: Broad angular head, pointed eyelid projections and a leaf-like snout and brown body. Females are larger than males. Projection length varies, so it should not be the only identification feature.
after.diet: Animal prey on the forest floor, including invertebrates and small vertebrates such as other frogs or lizards.
after.activity: Secretive; calls can be heard around dusk and were recorded during late-afternoon breeding observations in Singapore.
after.behaviour: Remains still in leaf litter and ambushes passing prey. Local researchers have often detected it by its distinctive loud call near streams.
after.reproduction: Breeds in forest streams. A Singapore field study recorded mating and a cluster of gelatinous eggs attached beneath partly submerged bark; larvae develop in water.
after.singapore: Associated with patches of mature forest in the Central Nature Reserves. It is nationally Critically Endangered in RDB3; this guide avoids breeding-site directions.
after.ecologicalRole: An ambush predator that connects leaf-litter prey with larger forest predators; its aquatic young also depend on stream habitat.
after.pressures: Loss or damage to moist forest and stream habitat is a concern, alongside collection for the pet trade across its range.
after.watch: Listen from open trails during permitted hours. Do not use call playback, move leaf litter, enter breeding streams or handle frogs and eggs.

after.name: Malayan porcupine
after.habitat: Mature forest
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.fact: Porcupines cannot shoot their quills. A quill can detach after contact, which helps explain the familiar myth.
after.summary: A large ground-dwelling rodent with striking defensive quills. Camera traps helped establish that this secretive native mammal still survived in Singapore after decades with few reports.
after.identification: A blunt muzzle, stout body, short legs and a short tail. The longest back quills are strongly patterned in black and white. It is a porcupine, not a hedgehog.
after.diet: Fruit, roots and stems, gathered while foraging on the ground.
after.activity: Nocturnal; normally shelters in burrows during daylight.
after.behaviour: Digs burrows and travels on land. A threatened animal can raise its quills, rattle its tail and back towards a threat; leave it room to retreat.
after.reproduction: Gives birth to live young. The Singapore field sources reviewed here do not establish a local breeding season or typical litter size, so no exact reproductive timetable is claimed.
after.singapore: Rediscovered on an offshore island in 2005. Later camera-trap records documented animals in mainland forest reserves and other wooded areas. RDB3 continues to recognise a native, nationally Critically Endangered population.
after.ecologicalRole: Its plant feeding links roots, stems and fallen fruit to the forest food web; burrowing also disturbs small patches of soil.
after.pressures: Forest loss and fragmentation reduce habitat. Hunting for meat and trade in body parts are documented regional pressures; the reviewed sources do not provide a current Singapore hunting rate.
after.watch: Keep a generous distance and never block its path or approach a burrow. Do not attempt to handle an animal or remove its quills.

after.name: Malayan water monitor

after.summary: A large lizard commonly seen beside Singapore’s water. It is an able swimmer, but can also walk on land and climb trees.

after.diet: Small animals, including fish, and carrion.
after.activity: Diurnal.
after.behaviour: Searches for food near water and may bask on banks. Its forked tongue samples chemical cues in the environment.

after.ecologicalRole: Both predator and scavenger in waterside food webs.
after.pressures: Unsafe encounters, road crossings and disturbance can affect animals living beside people.
after.watch: Give it space and a route away. Do not feed, touch or provoke it; a defensive bite can injure.

after.identification: A bushy tail and a pale stripe above a darker stripe on each flank are useful clues. Check side markings, rather than relying on coat colour alone.
after.diet: Fruit, seeds and other plant food, with some animal food.
after.activity: Diurnal.
after.behaviour: Uses claws to climb and makes quick leaps between branches. Chirps and chatter are part of its communication.

after.ecologicalRole: A seed and fruit consumer within tree-based food webs.
after.pressures: Loss of tree connections and feeding by people can affect normal movement and foraging.
after.watch: Enjoy it from the path. Do not bait it for a photograph or offer snacks.

after.name: Purple heron
after.habitat: Vegetated wetlands and marshes
after.rarity: Resident; easily hidden in dense wetland plants
after.globalStatus: Least Concern · assessed 2019
after.fact: Its elongated toes help it place careful steps on marsh plants and floating vegetation.
after.globalAssessmentNote: Assessment date and category verified through the IUCN SSC Heron Specialist Group’s Red List table (version 2024-2).
after.summary: A slender heron adapted to wetland vegetation. Its chestnut neck, dark lines and patient stillness make it less obvious among stems than its name might suggest.
after.identification: Adults have a long chestnut neck marked with dark stripes, a dark cap, greyish upperparts and a narrow pointed bill. Young birds are browner and lack the adult's strong neck markings. It is around 78–90 cm long.
after.diet: Fish are important prey, alongside frogs, aquatic invertebrates and other small animals; diet varies with habitat and prey availability.
after.activity: Often forages around morning and evening, but can also feed in daylight. Local observation times do not establish a fixed island-wide schedule.
after.behaviour: Waits among dense plants or moves slowly through shallow water to catch prey. Long toes help it negotiate emergent and floating vegetation.
after.reproduction: Builds a platform of reeds or sticks in wetland vegetation; trees and thickets can also be used. Both parents incubate and feed the young. Regional breeding seasons and clutch sizes vary, so none is presented here as a Singapore norm.
after.singapore: A resident species recorded in freshwater wetlands and coastal vegetation. NParks lists the Central Catchment, Sungei Buloh and Pulau Ubin. It can be familiar at suitable wetlands while remaining nationally Endangered.
after.ecologicalRole: A wetland predator linking small aquatic animals to the bird food web.
after.pressures: The Heron Specialist Group identifies wetland alteration and disturbance as pressures across its range. Retaining suitable vegetated feeding and nesting habitat is a relevant local priority; no current Singapore decline rate is asserted.
after.watch: Use hides and stay on public paths. Do not enter reedbeds, cut vegetation or flush a hidden bird into view. Keep nesting habitat undisturbed.

after.name: Raffles's banded langur
after.habitat: Mature forest canopy in the Central Catchment
after.fact: This arboreal leaf-eater digests vegetation in a multi-chambered stomach.

after.diet: Leaves, unripe fruit and other plant material.
after.activity: Mainly active during daylight in the canopy.
after.behaviour: Lives in social groups and spends much of its time in trees. Its specialised stomach supports digestion of leafy food.

after.ecologicalRole: A forest canopy herbivore, linked to the diversity of its food plants.
after.pressures: Small population size and fragmented forest make protection of habitat and connectivity important.
after.watch: Use open trails and binoculars. Do not follow a group off-trail, play calls or share sensitive locations.

after.habitat: Mature forest canopy
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.fact: Its broad, flattened tail gives the group its 'arrow-tailed flying squirrel' nickname.
after.summary: A tiny forest squirrel with warm-coloured cheeks and a broad gliding membrane. It is one of Singapore's least conspicuous mammals and needs careful observation to separate it from other gliders.
after.identification: Grey-brown upperparts with rusty colouring, a pale underside, orange-brown cheeks and a flattened tail. NParks describes a narrow white edge along the side of the gliding membrane.
after.diet: Regional observations describe fruit, flowers and leaves, with some insects.
after.activity: Nocturnal and mainly active in trees.
after.behaviour: Glides between trees and shelters in cavities in tall trunks. It appears largely solitary, but detailed social studies are limited.
after.reproduction: Uses sheltered tree holes. Reliable species-specific breeding dates and litter sizes were not established in this review. Frequently repeated numbers in one educational account are actually attributed to a different Hylopetes species.
after.singapore: Recorded from Bukit Timah and Central Catchment forests. The latter records were published in 2013, so the older statement that it occurs only in Bukit Timah is not retained.
after.ecologicalRole: Connects canopy plant resources and small invertebrates with the forest food web. No measured Singapore seed-dispersal rate is claimed.
after.pressures: Loss or degradation of mature forest can remove both food and cavity shelters. Its restricted habitat and small size also make monitoring difficult.
after.watch: Watch quietly from open trails without flash or prolonged direct light. Do not inspect occupied tree cavities or publish exact shelter locations.

after.identification: Usually brownish-grey with a darker face and tail, pale forehead marking and three dark lines along the back. Markings vary, so a quick glimpse is insufficient to identify an unfamiliar civet confidently.
after.diet: Fruit is important, alongside insects and small vertebrates. It belongs to the carnivore order but has an omnivorous diet.

after.ecologicalRole: A fruit eater and predator of small animals. Seed transport is a plausible ecological contribution, but the profile does not claim a measured local dispersal rate or a demonstrated keystone role.
after.pressures: Forest loss and degradation affect canopy habitat. The reviewed literature describes hunting and capture elsewhere in its range; it does not quantify current Singapore exploitation.
after.watch: Use binoculars from permitted paths and leave resting animals undisturbed. Never bait, feed, touch or follow a civet into the forest.

after.identification: A long brown body, short smooth fur and a paler throat and underside. It is larger than the Asian small-clawed otter; do not identify the species from size alone.
after.diet: Mainly fish, with other aquatic prey.
after.activity: Active on land and in water; sightings vary with the group and site.
after.behaviour: Travels and feeds in family groups. Groups use scent and calls and may compete with other families over territory.
after.reproduction: Pups are raised in sheltered dens, with adults attending them. Keep away from resting and den areas even if no adult is visible.
after.singapore: Uses mangroves, reservoirs, ponds and urban canals. Frequent sightings at one waterway do not change its national Endangered status.
after.ecologicalRole: An aquatic predator connecting waterways and adjacent land habitats.
after.pressures: Road crossings, disturbance and unsafe encounters can affect urban families. Connected, usable waterways remain important.
after.watch: Keep your distance and do not block the route between the group and water. Keep dogs leashed and never feed otters.

funFacts.text: Singapore now has breeding otter families using urban as well as natural waterways.

after.name: Spiny hill turtle
after.habitat: Mature forest
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.fact: Its dramatic juvenile shell edges become much less spiky as the turtle grows.
after.summary: A forest-floor turtle with an especially striking shell when young. Singapore's remaining mature forests shelter this locally Endangered reptile.
after.identification: Brown shell with a raised middle ridge and jagged rear edge; dark head and limbs, with reddish marks beside the head. Young turtles have much sharper shell-edge projections than adults.
after.diet: An omnivore. Regional research records fruit and other plant material, some animal food and mushrooms; the proportions in Singapore have not been measured here.
after.activity: NParks describes mainly nocturnal activity; this is not a rule that excludes daytime encounters.
after.behaviour: Adults spend much of their time on land. Younger turtles use water more extensively, so forest-floor and stream habitats both matter.
after.reproduction: Lays eggs. Breeding has been achieved in conservation collections; no Singapore nesting month or clutch-size claim is made here.
after.singapore: Native populations are associated with the Central Nature Reserves. The national assessment is Endangered in RDB3; encounter locations and resting sites are not mapped here.
after.ecologicalRole: Consumes material from several parts of the forest food web. Mushroom eating is documented, but effective fungal-spore dispersal by this species remains a research question.
after.pressures: Forest degradation and collection for trade threaten it. Protecting habitat and preventing collection are central conservation needs.
after.watch: Keep to open paths, leave it where it is and avoid handling or flash. Do not disclose a precise location or collect an animal for a pet.

after.name: Straw-headed bulbul
after.habitat: Dense foliage near rivers and forest edges
after.fact: Its loud song has made it a target of the illegal songbird trade.
after.globalStatus: Critically Endangered · 2018
after.summary: A large songbird whose voice often gives it away before its body appears. Singapore is important to its survival, while capture for the songbird trade has damaged populations elsewhere.
after.identification: A straw-coloured crown, dark facial stripes and pale streaks on the breast. It is larger than many familiar urban bulbuls.
after.diet: Fruit, berries and insects.
after.activity: Diurnal; often heard from dense vegetation.
after.behaviour: Forages in thick foliage near water and forest edges. Its loud, bubbling song is a useful clue, but listening must not become playback or disturbance.
after.reproduction: An egg-laying bird whose nesting cover needs protection. Do not seek nests or publish nest locations; local timing is not predicted by this guide.
after.singapore: Found in suitable wooded habitats, including Pulau Ubin. Local occurrence and its global Critically Endangered label refer to different geographic scales.
after.ecologicalRole: A fruit-eater and insect predator within wooded habitats.
after.pressures: Illegal capture for the songbird trade and habitat loss. Singapore’s species action plan includes habitat work and protection against poaching.
after.watch: Listen quietly from paths. Never play calls to draw it out, set up bait or publicise a nest.

funFacts.title: Heard before seen
funFacts.text: Its bubbling song can reveal a bird that stays hidden in dense leaves.

funFacts.title: A big bulbul

after.name: Sumatran palm civet
after.habitat: Woodland, gardens and some urban areas
after.rarity: Widespread but mostly hidden by day
after.fact: Seeds from fruit meals can be spread in a civet’s droppings.
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.summary: A nocturnal fruit-eater and small-animal hunter, often known locally as the common palm civet. It can move through both trees and settled areas in search of food.
after.identification: A long body and tail, pointed muzzle and dark facial markings. It is a civet, not a domestic cat despite the nickname ‘toddy cat’.
after.diet: Fruit, berries and small animals, including insects.
after.activity: Nocturnal; usually rests out of sight by day.
after.behaviour: Often forages alone, using branches and the ground. Adaptability allows it to visit gardens and buildings beside green spaces.
after.reproduction: Females give birth to dependent young in sheltered places. Avoid disturbing roof spaces or tree hollows occupied by a family.
after.singapore: A native resident of wooded areas and some neighbourhoods. The name Sumatran palm civet follows NParks’ current species table.
after.ecologicalRole: Passes seeds from eaten fruit, helping seed dispersal.
after.pressures: Road crossings, loss of shelter and conflict around homes. Wildlife-friendly coexistence is preferable to feeding or trapping.
after.watch: Secure food waste and allow it to leave. If young are present, seek AVS advice before closing an access hole.

funFacts.text: Seeds from fruit meals can be spread in a civet’s droppings.

after.name: Sunda colugo
after.habitat: Tall forest, nearby parkland and plantations
after.fact: Its broad patagium supports controlled glides between trees.
after.rarity: Restricted range; rarely seen, but locally common at some sites
after.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2008
after.summary: A tree specialist that travels on a sheet of skin. Colugos glide between trunks instead of flapping wings, and spend much of the day pressed quietly against bark.
after.identification: Look for mottled grey-brown fur, large eyes, curved claws and a broad membrane joining the limbs and tail. The folded membrane can be hard to see on a resting animal.
after.diet: Young leaves, shoots, flowers and fruit.
after.activity: Mainly nocturnal; rests on trees by day.
after.behaviour: Climbs to gain height before a glide. Camouflage and stillness help it stay unnoticed. It is neither a bat nor a true lemur.
after.reproduction: Usually one young is born. The infant clings to its mother; she can fold her gliding membrane around it for support and warmth.
after.singapore: Associated with tall forest in the Central Nature Reserves and connected wooded spaces. A quiet, hidden animal may be present even when visitors do not notice it.
after.ecologicalRole: A canopy herbivore that links plant growth to the forest food web.
after.pressures: Loss of connected tree cover reduces feeding areas and routes through the canopy.
after.watch: Stay on open trails. Use binoculars and avoid flash or shining a light into its eyes.

funFacts.title: A blanket that glides
funFacts.text: A mother can fold her gliding membrane into a pouch around her young.

funFacts.title: Flying in name only
funFacts.text: The ‘flying lemur’ is neither a lemur nor a powered flier.

after.name: Sunda pangolin
after.habitat: Forests and vegetated corridors
after.fact: Large claws open ant and termite nests; a sticky tongue gathers prey.
after.globalStatus: Critically Endangered · 2019
after.summary: Singapore’s native pangolin is a shy, scale-covered mammal. It searches for social insects on the ground and in trees, using strong claws and a long sticky tongue.
after.identification: Overlapping brown scales, a narrow head, a long tail and powerful digging claws. Its underside has softer skin and hair.
after.diet: Ants and termites; it opens their nests to reach them.
after.activity: Mostly nocturnal and secretive.
after.behaviour: Can climb trees as well as walk on the ground. When frightened it rolls up, protecting its softer underside with scales.
after.reproduction: Usually has one baby at a time. Young may ride on the mother’s tail or back while she moves.
after.singapore: Recorded in forested areas, including the Central Catchment and offshore islands. Exact resting sites are deliberately excluded from this guide.
after.ecologicalRole: A specialised predator of ants and termites within forest food webs.
after.pressures: Road collisions and habitat loss matter locally. Wildlife trafficking is a major threat across its wider range.
after.watch: Give it a clear escape route. Do not touch, corner or pick it up; contact AVS if it is injured or trapped.

funFacts.title: A tiny passenger
funFacts.text: A young pangolin can hitch a ride on its mother’s back or tail.

funFacts.title: Built-in protection
funFacts.text: Its defensive curl puts tough scales outside and its soft belly inside.

after.name: Sunda slow loris
after.habitat: Forest canopy in nature reserves and Pulau Tekong
after.fact: Large, forward-facing eyes support its activity at night.
after.globalStatus: Endangered · 2020
after.summary: A nocturnal primate that moves carefully through branches. Its deliberate movement, strong grip and large eyes suit a life in the dark canopy.
after.identification: Rounded head, large forward-facing eyes, dense fur and a dark stripe along the back. The tail is very short and usually hidden.
after.diet: Tree gums and sap, nectar and small animal prey including insects.
after.activity: Nocturnal; rests out of sight during daylight.
after.behaviour: Moves hand over hand and can hold branches for long periods. A slow movement style does not make it safe to handle: it has a venomous bite.
after.reproduction: Females usually produce a single infant and provide prolonged care. Young depend on their mother before foraging independently.
after.singapore: A rare forest resident recorded in the nature reserves and Pulau Tekong. This guide withholds precise observation and resting locations.
after.ecologicalRole: Feeds across plant and small-animal parts of the canopy food web.
after.pressures: Habitat loss and the illegal pet trade affect slow lorises. Connected forest and freedom from disturbance are important.
after.watch: Never touch or attempt to rescue one by hand. Do not use flash photography or lure it into view.

funFacts.title: A surprising primate
funFacts.text: The slow loris is venomous; its gentle appearance does not mean it is safe to handle.

funFacts.title: Branch by branch
funFacts.text: Strong hands and feet let it move carefully through the canopy without big leaps.

after.name: White-bellied sea eagle
after.habitat: Reservoirs, rivers and coastlines
after.fact: Broad wings form a shallow V while it soars above waterways.
after.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2022
after.summary: A large coastal raptor often seen circling above Singapore’s water. Adult and young birds look quite different, so a brown eagle is not automatically another species.
after.identification: Adults have a white head and underside with grey upperparts. Young birds are mottled brown. Broad wings are held in a shallow V when soaring.
after.diet: Fish and other animals taken around waterways; also scavenges.
after.activity: Diurnal, often soaring above water.
after.behaviour: Uses rising air to soar while looking for food. Pairs build large stick nests in suitable tall trees.
after.reproduction: Both adults help with nesting and care for chicks. Nests may be reused and enlarged over successive years.
after.singapore: Occurs around reservoirs, rivers and the coast. It can be observed from many public waterfronts without approaching a nest.
after.ecologicalRole: A high-level predator and scavenger associated with aquatic food webs.
after.pressures: Protecting large nesting trees and limiting disturbance helps keep suitable habitat available.
after.watch: Use binoculars from a safe viewpoint. Never fly a drone near a nest or move closer to force a take-off.

funFacts.title: A growing home
funFacts.text: A pair can keep adding sticks to a nest that it uses again.

funFacts.title: A different youngster
funFacts.text: Brown juvenile plumage changes gradually into the adult white-and-grey pattern.

after.name: Wild boar
after.habitat: Forest, scrub and adjoining green spaces
after.rarity: Regular in suitable habitat; varies by site
after.fact: Piglets have pale stripes that become less obvious as they grow.
after.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
after.summary: One of Singapore’s largest land mammals. Its strong snout turns leaf litter and soil while it searches for food, so disturbed ground can be a clue to its presence.
after.identification: A stocky body with coarse dark hair, an elongated snout and short legs. Young piglets have pale lengthwise stripes that fade with age.
after.diet: Roots, fruit and other plant parts, plus invertebrates and carrion.
after.activity: Can be active by day or night; timing changes with disturbance.
after.behaviour: Roots through the ground for food. Females may travel with young; an animal with piglets or no escape route needs particular space.
after.reproduction: Females give birth to litters and nurse their piglets. Young follow their mother after an early period in shelter.
after.singapore: Occurs in forests and adjoining green areas, and may enter urban spaces. Encounter frequency varies greatly between places.
after.ecologicalRole: An omnivore whose rooting changes soil and leaf litter.
after.pressures: Human food, roads and encounters near urban edges can lead to conflict. Never encourage it to approach people.
after.watch: Stay calm, keep your distance and avoid separating adults from piglets. Do not feed or corner a boar.

funFacts.title: Stripy beginnings
funFacts.text: Piglets have pale stripes that become less obvious as they grow.

funFacts.title: A nose for a meal
funFacts.text: Its snout is a useful digging tool for roots and hidden food.

after.question: About how many native bat species does the AVS Singapore guide report?
after.explanation: NParks notes that Singapore has about 25 bat species, all native to the country.
after.hint: It is more than twenty but fewer than thirty.

after.question: A Singapore guide lists 429 bird species. Can you use that number as a bird population count?

answers.label: No. It counts species, not individual birds
Yes. It means exactly 429 birds live in Singapore
Yes. Each park must contain 429 birds
Yes. It counts only individual native birds

after.explanation: Species richness counts distinct species. It does not state how many individual birds live in Singapore.
after.hint: Check what the number measures.

after.question: What has driven the Straw-headed bulbul's severe decline across much of Southeast Asia?
after.explanation: Its prized bubbling song has made the species a major target of trapping and illegal trade; Singapore remains an important stronghold.
after.hint: The threat is linked to the bird's distinctive voice.

after.question: Civets are more closely related to which animals than to cats?
after.explanation: Despite the name 'civet cat', civets are more closely related to mongooses than to cats.
after.hint: Choose another small carnivoran with a long body and tail.

after.question: Which reef zone has the highest density of marine life, according to NParks?
after.explanation: NParks states that the submerged reef crest has the highest density of marine life.
after.hint: It lies between the flat and slope.

after.question: Why should a reef survey record depth and reef zone when comparing marine communities?

answers.label: Depth and light affect which communities occur in each zone
Every zone supports the same community at the same density
Only the reef flat contains living organisms
Every zone is exposed to air at each low tide

after.explanation: Reef flats, crests and slopes support different communities. Depth and available light affect these patterns.
after.hint: Compare the conditions on a shallow flat and a deeper slope.

after.question: Which animal is endemic to Singapore, meaning it is found nowhere else in the wild?
after.explanation: The Singapore freshwater crab, Johora singaporensis, is unique to Singapore.
after.hint: Its place name is part of both its common and scientific names.

after.question: At which Singapore park have female hawksbill turtles been recorded coming ashore to lay eggs?
after.explanation: Female hawksbill turtles have been recorded nesting along Singapore's coast, including East Coast Park.
after.hint: Choose the park with a long marine shoreline.

after.question: What typically happens while an Oriental pied hornbill female nests?

answers.label: She stays in a mostly sealed tree cavity
She nests on an open branch

after.explanation: The female and chicks stay inside a tree hole sealed with mud and fibres, leaving a narrow opening for food from the male.
after.hint: Large old trees can provide an important hollow space.

after.question: Which hornbill is a resident bird in Singapore?
after.explanation: The Oriental pied hornbill is Singapore's native resident hornbill and a well-known conservation comeback.
after.hint: Look for the black-and-white bird with a pale bill and casque.

after.question: What evidence did NUS researchers use to build a population baseline for three Asian horseshoe crab species?
after.explanation: The NUS team used genome-wide DNA evidence to study genetic diversity, past ranges and possible future conservation pressures.
after.hint: The study examined inherited information in DNA.

after.question: A mangrove horseshoe crab belongs to which broad animal group?
after.explanation: Horseshoe crabs are chelicerates, not true crabs; they share their broader group with spiders and scorpions.
after.hint: Its common name is misleading.

after.question: Which bird may raise an Asian koel chick?

answers.label: A House Crow or Large-billed Crow

after.explanation: Asian koels lay eggs in House Crow or Large-billed Crow nests. The host parents raise the chicks.
after.hint: This koel uses another bird’s nest.

after.question: What is Singapore’s most common non-human primate?
after.explanation: AVS identifies the Long-tailed macaque as Singapore’s most common non-human primate.
after.hint: It is also called the Crab-eating macaque.

after.question: Besides forests, which habitat can Long-tailed macaques use naturally?
after.explanation: Long-tailed macaques naturally live in forested areas and can also be found in mangroves.
after.hint: It is a coastal forest habitat.

after.question: What forest service can long-tailed macaques provide after eating fruit?
after.explanation: Seeds carried or passed after fruit is eaten can be moved away from the parent plant.
after.hint: Think about what happens to the seeds inside a fruit.

after.question: Why can feeding macaques disrupt their role in forests?

answers.label: It can draw them away from natural foraging and seed dispersal
It always increases the number of forest seeds they disperse
It changes where they eat but cannot affect forest plants
It affects seed dispersal only during rain

after.explanation: Human food can draw macaques away from forest foraging. This can disrupt the seed dispersal they provide.
after.hint: Think about where the macaques find their food.

after.question: Which of Singapore's monitor lizards is the most common?
after.explanation: The Malayan water monitor is the monitor lizard most commonly encountered in Singapore.
after.hint: It is often seen close to canals, ponds and reservoirs.

after.question: What conservation problem does Eco-Link@BKE help address?

answers.label: The expressway separated two forest reserves
Tides isolated a coral reef from a mangrove
A lack of artificial nest boxes in both reserves
A need to feed forest animals at fixed stations

after.explanation: Eco-Link@BKE reconnects Bukit Timah and Central Catchment reserves to support animal movement and seed dispersal.
after.hint: Consider how roads divide habitat.

after.explanation: The AVS guide mentions up to about eight minutes. This is a reported upper limit, not a typical dive duration for every otter.

after.question: Which squirrel is most commonly encountered in Singapore's urban parks and gardens?
